lead: A microprocessor is a complete CPU on one silicon chip. A microcontroller is that CPU plus program memory, data memory, timers and input/output ports on the same chip, so it runs alone. Transistors kept shrinking, so data paths widened from 4 bits to 64 bits, and then whole systems moved onto one chip. The microprocessor sits in a laptop or server; the microcontroller sits in a washing machine, a bike's engine controller, a UPI card reader and a smart meter.
prereq: You need only the everyday idea of a computer as something that takes input, processes it and gives output; the CPU, memory and bus picture comes next in 1.2.

blocks.text: The central processing unit (CPU) fetches an instruction from memory, decodes it and executes it. It holds a few very fast storage slots called registers, and an arithmetic logic unit (ALU) that adds, subtracts and does logic. Everything else in the machine feeds the CPU or carries away its results. The fetch-decode-execute loop is in 1.3.

A microprocessor (MPU) is a CPU on one silicon chip, and nothing more. Its pins go out to three buses: address, data and control. Program memory, data memory, timers and input/output (I/O) ports are separate chips wired to those buses. The 8085 and 8086 are microprocessors. 1.2 draws the buses.

A microcontroller (MCU) is a CPU plus the rest of a small computer on the same chip: program memory (ROM or flash), data memory (RAM), timers and counters, I/O ports and usually a serial port. It runs a program with no outside chips. The 8051 is the classic example.

An embedded system is a computer hidden inside a product to do one fixed job, where the product is not sold as a computer: a washing machine, a fuel-injection unit, an inverter. Such products must be cheap, small and low-power, so hiding the whole computer in one chip is the only way that makes sense.

Bit width is the number of bits the ALU and main registers handle in one operation; it is also called the word size. An 8-bit CPU adds two 8-bit numbers at a time; a 64-bit CPU adds two 64-bit numbers.

items: 4-bit: the Intel 4004 in 1971, built for calculators, about 2,300 transistors.
8-bit: the Intel 8080 in 1974 and 8085 in 1976, which powered early personal computers and instruments.
16-bit: the Intel 8086 in 1978, with 20 address lines reaching 1 MB; its twin the 8088 went into the first IBM PC.
32-bit: the Intel 80386 in 1985, which brought protected memory and multitasking operating systems.
64-bit: the early 2000s, making more than 4 GB of RAM directly addressable.

blocks.text: Two forces drove this: transistors shrinking, roughly doubling devices per area every two years (Moore's law), and each wider data path finishing more work per instruction.

Microcontrollers grew separately: the 8048, the 8051 in 1980, then PIC, AVR and ARM Cortex-M. Many stay at 8 or 16 bits, because a washing machine needs no 64-bit arithmetic and narrow buses waste less power.
Since the 2010s the lines merge in the system on chip (SoC): CPU, graphics unit, memory controller and radio blocks on one die, as in a phone.
The exam question is always the same: given a job, pick one and justify it. Work down this table.

head: Feature
Microprocessor
Microcontroller
rows: MHz to a few hundred MHz

blocks.text: Read the table by columns. A microprocessor is built for speed, so it burns watts and needs a fan. A microcontroller is built for cost, size and power, so it runs for years on a small cell.
One warning: bit width is not memory size. The number of address lines fixes how much memory the CPU can name.

blocks.where: M is the number of directly addressable byte locations and n is the number of address lines on the address bus.

blocks.text: An 8086 is a 16-bit CPU with 20 address lines, so M = 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 bytes = 1 MB. Two different numbers for two different jobs. Memory chips are covered in 1.5.

figure.caption: The upper branch is only a CPU, so memory and I/O are separate chips; the lower branch has ROM, RAM, timers and ports on one die.

spec.aria: A tree splits processors into microprocessors, which need external memory and I/O, and microcontrollers, which include ROM, RAM, timers and I/O ports on one chip.

examples.question: An 8051-based washing-machine board carries a CPU, 4 KB of program ROM, 128 B of RAM, two timers and 32 I/O pins on one chip. A desktop board carries an 8086 CPU plus one RAM chip, one ROM chip holding the firmware, one timer chip and one I/O controller chip. (a) Classify each board, giving two reasons each. (b) Count the chips on each board. (c) Find the total on-chip memory of the 8051 board in bytes.
steps: 8051 board: CPU, ROM, RAM, timers and I/O ports all sit on one die. A device with a CPU plus on-chip memory and peripherals is a microcontroller. Reason 1: it works as a complete computer in one chip. Reason 2: program memory and I/O ports are already inside it.

8086 board: the 8086 is a CPU only, and RAM, ROM, timer and I/O are separate chips on the system bus. That is a microprocessor system. Reason 1: the processor chip is CPU-only. Reason 2: memory and peripherals are off-chip.
Chip count, 8051 board: everything on one die, so 1 chip.
Chip count, 8086 board: 1 CPU + 1 RAM + 1 ROM + 1 timer + 1 I/O = 5 chips.
On-chip ROM in bytes: 4 KB × 1024 B per KB = 4096 B.
Add on-chip RAM: 4096 B + 128 B = 4224 B.
examples.answer: The 8051 board is a microcontroller (1 chip, 4224 B of on-chip memory); the 8086 board is a microprocessor system (5 chips).

examples.question: A 16-bit CPU has 20 address lines. How many bytes can it address directly, and how does that differ from its bit width?
steps: Bit width is 16 bits: the ALU adds 16-bit numbers in one operation.
So the CPU works on 16-bit data but names 1 MB of memory; the two numbers answer different questions.
examples.answer: It addresses 2²⁰ = 1,048,576 bytes, that is 1 MB, while its data width stays 16 bits.

traps: Calling any small CPU a microcontroller. A microcontroller must carry on-chip program memory, data memory and peripherals; a chip with only a CPU is a microprocessor, however small.
Equating bit width with addressable memory. The 8086 is 16-bit but has 20 address lines, so it reaches 1 MB, not 64 KB.
Mixing up the 8085 and the 8051. The 8085 is an 8-bit microprocessor with no on-chip program memory; the 8051 is an 8-bit microcontroller with 4 KB ROM and 128 B RAM inside.
Saying a microprocessor has no memory. It has on-chip registers; what it lacks is on-chip program and data memory.
Assuming a higher clock always wins. A 3 GHz desktop CPU and a 12 MHz 8051 do different jobs; the microcontroller wins on power, size and cost per unit.

quiz.q: Define microprocessor and microcontroller in one sentence each.
quiz.a: A microprocessor is a CPU on a single chip, with memory, timers and I/O as external chips. A microcontroller is a CPU with program memory, data memory, timers and I/O ports integrated on the same chip.

quiz.q: Name the first 4-bit microprocessor and its year.
quiz.a: The Intel 4004, in 1971, built for calculators.

quiz.q: Why can a microcontroller run a program with no external memory chip while a microprocessor cannot?
quiz.a: The microcontroller's die already holds flash or ROM for the program, RAM for data and the ports to talk outside. The microprocessor has only registers and bus pins, so program and data memory must be wired to it as separate chips.

quiz.q: Explain why bit width and addressable memory size are not the same thing.
quiz.a: Bit width is the number of bits the ALU and registers handle in one operation, setting data precision. Addressable memory is set by the address lines: M = 2ⁿ bytes. The 8086 handles 16-bit data but has 20 address lines, so it names 1 MB.

quiz.q: An 8051 has 4 KB of flash and 128 B of RAM on chip. What is its total on-chip memory in bytes?
A CPU has 16 address lines. How many bytes can it address directly?
quiz.a: M = 2ⁿ with n = 16, so M = 65,536 byte locations = 64 KB.

quiz.q: A designer must build a battery-run toy that blinks LEDs, reads one push button and must cost very little in bulk. Choose microprocessor or microcontroller and give three reasons.
quiz.a: Microcontroller. One: CPU, memory, timer and I/O are on a single chip, so the board needs almost no other parts and the cost per unit stays low. Two: it draws milliwatts, so small cells last long. Three: the job needs only 8-bit arithmetic and a few KB of program, which an 8051-class part provides; a microprocessor would add external RAM, ROM and I/O chips, raising cost, size and power for no gain.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the split has blurred: a phone SoC carries eight or more CPU cores, a GPU, a memory controller and radio blocks on one die, while a low-cost sensor node uses an ARM Cortex-M class microcontroller that sleeps in microamps. Open-source cores such as RISC-V now let a company design its own microcontroller without a licence fee, which is changing the low-cost end of the market. Coursework increasingly adds low-power modes, interrupt latency and security features such as a trust zone.
